newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Albright leads trio of NATO leaders to Russia.
newsitem.headline: Albright leads trio of NATO leaders to Russia.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright arrives in Russia on Saturday, leading a trio of NATO foreign ministers visiting in quick succession to keep up the momentum in improving relations with Moscow.

Albright will meet Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov in St Petersburg during a visit lasting less than 24 hours to assure him about the implications of NATO enlargement and discuss arms control.
It was not clear if Russian objections to a NATO swoop on suspected war criminals in Bosnia, which Moscow denounced on Friday as "cowboy raids", would be raised.
Primakov will then return to Moscow for meetings early next week with new British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook and German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel.
Western diplomats have played down the direct links between the trips.
But all three visitors were expected to address Russian fears about NATO enlargement and explore ways to develop a new partnership pact between Moscow and the defence alliance.
"The aim of the talks is to continue to develop the personal ties at the top level, but NATO will obviously be on the agenda," said one Western diplomat in Moscow.

President Bill Clinton, Albright and other American leaders have fanned out across formerly communist eastern Europe to accept accolades from the states invited to join NATO this week and to reassure those left out.
Russia reiterated its opposition when the Western defence alliance issued membership invitations to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic at a summit in Madrid.
But Russian officials say they want to build on the improvement in relations with their former Cold War foe that culminated in the NATO-Russia partnership pact in May.
That accord gave Moscow a say, but not a veto, in some NATO-related security matters.

"We are realists and we live in a real world. NATO exists and we cannot ignore that. It would be a great mistake to do so," deputy prime minister Valery Serov, who represented Russia in Madrid, told a news conference on Friday.
Pledging Russia to cooperation, he said: "I think that attempts to revive confrontation are the worst way, and a hopeless way, to go."
Albright is visiting Russia as part of a trip also taking in Slovenia and the former Soviet republic of Lithuania, both of which hope eventually to join NATO.
She will have dinner with Primakov on Saturday and meet him at her hotel on Sunday.
U.S. officials say Albright wants to encourage Russia to take full advantage of the possibilities of the partnership pact with NATO, which encouraged Moscow to ease its resistance to expansion.

She and Primakov would also discuss arms control issues, including international negotiations on updating a 1990 treaty which limits the numbers of conventional arms in Europe and where they can be placed, they said.
They were also expected to discuss the START 2 nuclear arms agreement reducing strategic nuclear warheads. The pact has not been ratified by the Russian parliament.

Cook will be in Moscow on Monday and Tuesday on his first trip to Russia as foreign secretary. Western diplomats said he would discuss NATO and other matters with Primakov and also meet First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov.
Kinkel will meet Primakov next Tuesday before presiding at the opening a chocolate factory. Officials said NATO would be on the agenda at the talks but gave no details.
